Big modules should be split into submodules, pieces, or directories with composition once they grow past a certain size.

Ensure every system is indexed properly so nothing ever becomes impossible to find, and so I can see all the systems that are working.
Write down a to-do for a systematic systems audit: treat each module as a whole system, figure out what it is and does, read its READMEs, and assess its state (useful? move? rename? merge?).
Do the audit in a systematic way that seeks clarity and better organization, not rushed or random additions and removals, so that it actually improves things.
Write down only the important things with real influence; do not write obvious, expected, or irrelevant things, and prune obvious content.
Where should the systems audit notes go so we can always find them?
Capture as much session data as possible from the AI sessions, since they record the SDK creating the sessions.

Make READMEs reference on-demand notes that are summarized when injected, so each agent can load the full referenced README if relevant.
When building, editing, designing, or even bug fixing, most of the module's READMEs are probably relevant.
Keep READMEs small.
Consider universal page templates, since we probably should have them.
Show README size in tokens on any page and on the session page, computed for any module path, since we pay per token.
Can the SDK report the token count of the READMEs?
If the core page README system has a million tokens of READMEs, that is far too much.
A total README token measure across all sub-READMEs is useful, but they do not all have to be loaded at once.
How is it configured which READMEs get read; does the mastermind decide?
A mastermind can pass exactly which documentation a spawned minion should read, so the minion is aware of those systems.
Have any mastermind, in any directory, automatically read the READMEs on startup and flag anything massively out of place before the task begins.
Create improvements.md (or proposal.md) in directories where agents can recommend improvements, and link to it from the README.
Have a mastermind on startup review improvements; if an improvement has been recommended a couple of times, or is a quick fix that helps the system, do it before starting the next task.

Set up a logged tool for agents to read a README, so the session log shows which READMEs were read, which lets us trust agent judgment.
A mastermind that has read all READMEs can properly assess which parts of the system an agent will need to fix or build something.
Specifying READMEs through the mastermind is one strategy, but we still need to see which READMEs were loaded.
Do as much as possible in node so it happens automatically; do not rely on agents to remember.
Allow a mastermind spawning an agent to specify the exact sub-READMEs it should read, beyond the path and automatic injection, so the agent does not read too many.
Leave the choice of READMEs to the mastermind per spawn rather than configuring READMEs per role.

Agents may load additional READMEs, but start with the prescribed ones. Read order: all READMEs above the working path top-down, then the working directory's README, then the sub-READMEs the mastermind specifies.
The mastermind should read most READMEs, or at least be aware of them, even if it thinks it needs none.
Do token accounting for README systems in layers (each README's size, then referenced READMEs, then deeper levels), and show session-level context percentages for system prompt versus READMEs.
Decide carefully what goes in claude.md, and show what is removed or moved into the framework versus what stays.
How do we identify what should go in claude.md?
Move as much as possible into the framework README, since claude.md was not big and the framework README may not be used much.
The framework should not be locked into Claude; claude.md should hold only Claude-specific things, possibly a single line like 'read framework/readme'.
Give me an overview of the things I'm asking for.
Merges are my decision.
Make merges visible to me so I can see them.
Before a session can be completed, all of its tasks must be finished, and merging the work back in should be one of the tasks.
Any code change must go through our coding systems, the skills system that is becoming a README system.
Get an overview of all the roles, the skills each role needs, how they are defined, and how they are loaded, including which skills are invoked when minions are spawned.
Moving these things around is very prone to breaking, so it must be handled carefully.
Move toward a generic log tool that takes a string kind and arbitrary data, writing to session.jsonl, instead of logging all skill usage.
Do not log every file read and write, but do log spawning agents.
Spawn a minion to study the systems and find the best way to log everything.
We have too many tools, around 80 or 90.
Compact the tools into one item tool that takes a method and arbitrary data, like a remote procedure call, and do past-work research on the earlier compaction proposal.
Should the item tool log to page.jsonl or session.jsonl, and should the item be instantiated before logging?

One option is to instantiate the item server-side, apply the tool's delta, and save through a store adapter on the server instead of the socket, which allows validation and programmatic handling but is complicated.
Write down the future direction of the item system in the right place.
Map the item system, which is spread across many places, so that whoever looks at tool and skill usage can see it.
The direction is moving from skills to README-based prompt injection, then from that to tool-based prompt injection.
When a tool is used by the Claude harness, can it give an asynchronous response, with a request-response system that matches the eventual result to the original request?
Tool responses could be programmatic and automatic, based on instructions for that tool, so a skill-like tool returns instructions, and an item tool could have a help method.
Help me think this through: the ideas about skills, READMEs, prompt injection, and tool-based injection.
Only the necessary prompt injection should be used, since context management matters.
Can we hook into pre-tool-use prompt injection, so a tool use such as a file move reminds the agent of certain things?
This could be built into the tool description, or handled another way.
Per-tool-use reminders should be short and remind of the sequence of steps, like an operating procedure.
Firm sequences of steps should be managed programmatically through a loop or code-based control, not left to a reminder the AI has to follow.
